title: Streaming Price Index: Are Streaming Prices Rising Faster Than Inflation? | Streaming Price Tracker

Streaming Price Index: Are Streaming Prices Rising Faster Than Inflation? | Streaming Price Tracker

 The complete monthly price history of every major US streaming service, from Netflix, Disney+, and HBO Max to live TV services like YouTube TV, Sling TV, and fuboTV. The complete monthly price history of every major US streaming service. 

 Updated Nov 2026 Light theme 

# Streaming Price Index

US streaming prices are up 91% since 2019, versus 34% general inflation and 29% for cable and satellite TV.

 A monthly index of what US streaming services charge, built from 20 tracked plans across 9 on-demand services and measured the way official inflation statistics are. January 2019 = 100. Current through October 2026. 

Streaming, on demand +90.7% 8 plans in 2019, 20 today

Streaming, live TV +110.4% Cable replacement services

All items (CPI) +34.1% US consumer price inflation

Cable & satellite TV (CPI) +29.4% The thing streaming replaced

- Streaming +91%
- All items (CPI) +34%
- Cable & satellite TV (CPI) +29%

 January 2019 = 100. Streaming is the index described below; the two CPI series are published by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, not seasonally adjusted. CPI is released about six weeks in arrears, so all series stop at the most recent month every one of them covers. The CPI lines break where the BLS published no figure: October 2025 was not published because of the lapse in appropriations. It is left as a gap rather than filled in. 

## What the index says

 Streaming prices did almost nothing for a decade and then moved sharply. The on-demand index sat below its 2019 level for most of the 2010s, and was still only 100 in January 2021. Nearly all of the increase has landed since then, as most major services moved to ad-supported tiers and raised the price of ad-free ones. The steepest January-to-January rise was 2023 to 2024, at +16.8%. 

 Over the same months, general US inflation ran +34.1% and cable and satellite television, the product streaming was supposed to undercut, ran +29.4%. Streaming has been inflating about 2.7 times as fast as the economy as a whole and about 3.1 times as fast as cable. Live TV streaming, which competes with cable directly, has risen 110.4%.

Download the full monthly series (CSV), read the underlying price history, or see what every service charges today. 

## How it is calculated

 The index is a chained, matched-model index, the same family of formula the Bureau of Labor Statistics uses for the elementary parts of CPI. Each month it does this: 

1. Take every tracked plan that has a price in both this month and last month, and work out how much that specific plan changed. 
2. Average those changes within each service, so a service with four tracked tiers does not outweigh one with a single plan. 
3. Average across services, then multiply the running level by that month's result. Averages are geometric, which is what BLS uses at this level of CPI. 
4. Rescale the whole series so January 2019 reads 100.

 Comparing only plans present in both months is the part that matters. It means a service launching, or a plan being retired, never moves the index by itself. That is not a detail: most of the services on this site launched during the period being measured, so a simple average of current prices would rise steeply on lineup changes alone, before any price had gone up. 

 Add-on fees are excluded, because an add-on is not a subscription. Discontinued plans count for the months they were actually sold and then drop out. Live TV is indexed separately, since it substitutes for cable rather than for Netflix. A month's price is the price in effect at the end of that month. 

 The on-demand basket held 8 plans from 5 services in January 2019 and holds 20 plans from 9 services today: Netflix (3 plans): Standard with Ads, Standard, Premium; Disney+ (2 plans): Basic (with ads), Premium (no ads); Hulu (2 plans): With Ads, No Ads; ESPN (2 plans): Select (formerly ESPN+), Unlimited; HBO Max (3 plans): Basic With Ads, Standard, Premium; Apple TV (one plan): Monthly; Peacock (3 plans): Premium (with ads), Premium Plus (no ads), Select (with ads, limited content); Paramount+ (2 plans): Essential (with ads), Premium; Prime Video (2 plans): Standalone (with ads), Standalone (ad-free). 

## What this number does not mean

- It measures list prices, not bills. The index tracks advertised monthly prices for individual plans. It does not know about bundles, annual plan discounts, promotional rates, or the fact that people cancel and re-subscribe. A household's actual streaming spend can move very differently. 
- Every service counts equally. Apple TV carries the same weight as Netflix, because this site has price data and no subscriber data. A subscriber-weighted index would give a different number. 
- There is no quality adjustment. CPI tries to account for products changing over time. This index does not. Catalogues grew and shrank, 4K and simultaneous-stream limits moved, and password sharing was restricted, all within the measured period. Some of the price increase bought something. 
- Where you start counting changes the answer. The headline uses January 2019 because it sits just before the streaming-wars launches. Other starting points give other numbers, listed below. 
- The comparison stops where the data stops. BLS publishes each month's CPI in the middle of the following month, so every series here is cut to October 2026, the most recent month all of them cover.

## Sources and reuse

 Streaming prices come from this site's own tracked data, where every price carries at least two source citations. See how the data is sourced or browse the full price history. 

 Inflation figures are the US Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers, not seasonally adjusted: series `CUUR0000SA0` (all items) and `CUUR0000SERA02` (cable and satellite television service). BLS data is in the public domain. October 2025 was not published because of the lapse in appropriations and is left as a gap. 

 The index series is free to reuse under CC BY 4.0 with attribution to Streaming Price Tracker. Download the monthly series as CSV. 

## Streaming price index FAQ

### Is streaming getting more expensive?

Yes. The Streaming Price Index, which tracks 20 on-demand plans across 9 services, has risen 90.7% between January 2019 and October 2026. Prices were broadly flat until 2021 and have climbed steadily since. The steepest January-to-January rise was 2023 to 2024, when the index rose 16.8%.

### Are streaming prices rising faster than inflation?

Yes, by roughly 2.7 times. Since January 2019 the streaming index is +90.7% while the US Consumer Price Index for all items is +34.1% over the same months. A streaming subscription that tracked general inflation instead would cost about 30% less today than it does.

### How much have streaming prices gone up since 2019?

The on-demand index is up 90.7% since January 2019. Live TV streaming services have risen 110.4% over the same period. These are changes in advertised list prices, measured plan by plan, not changes in what the average household spends in total.

### Are streaming prices rising faster than cable prices?

Yes. Cable and satellite television prices rose 29.4% since January 2019, while streaming rose 90.7% over the same months, roughly 3.1 times as fast. The index compares how fast prices changed, not price levels, so it does not say which costs less.

### How is the Streaming Price Index calculated?

It is a chained, matched-model index, the same family of formula the US Bureau of Labor Statistics uses for CPI. Each month it compares the price of every plan against that same plan's price the previous month, averages those changes within each service and then across services, and chains the result into a running level set to 100 in January 2019. Comparing only matched plans month to month is what keeps a new service launching, or an old plan being retired, from moving the index on its own.

### Why not just average the price of every streaming service?

Because that number measures the lineup as much as the prices. Most major services launched during the period this site tracks, so a straight average of current prices rises simply because more, and more expensive, services exist. An index compares each plan only against itself.
